title: Legacy opt.converged()
body:
Move current `converged(gradient)` to `gradient_converged(gradient)` and add legacy-style `opt.converged(forces=None)` ensuring it is tested.

Closes #1744 #1878

comments.author: yuzie007
comments.body:
Thank you @askhl for the MR!

I have not fully followed the old and the present behaviors of `opt.converged()`, so likely I miss the point, but I get a naive question.

I was wondering what the actual issue is, then reading #1878, and noticed that, in their `ase_adsorption_finder_mol.py`, they did
```python
forces = system.get_forces()
...
if relax.converged(forces):
```
which, if I understand correctly, can actually simply be replaced with
```python
if relax.converged():
```
with rather reverting the `gradient=None` default like
```python
    def converged(self, gradient=None):
        """Did the optimization converge?"""
        if gradient is None:
            gradient = self.optimizable.get_gradient()
        assert gradient.ndim == 1
        return self.optimizable.converged(gradient, self.fmax)
```
Was there any issue with the `gradient=None` default?
comments.label_reasoning: The comment questions whether the API behavior (requiring gradient argument vs defaulting to None) matches the intended use case, suggesting the current design may not align with user intent.

review_threads.actionability_reasoning: Suggests an alternative implementation with gradient=None default, implying the current approach could be replaced with a simpler one.

comments.author: ajjackson
comments.body:
If I understand correctly, the proposed MR:
- renames the "new-style" `converged(gradient)` method to `gradient_converged(forces)` on the `Dynamics` class and some derived optimisers.
- implements a wrapper to restore the "old-style" `converged(forces=None)` on the `Optimizer` class (i.e. it is not available on other `Dynamics` - but in practice all `Dynamics` are optimizers anyway.)

This would break code that inherits `Dynamics` (rather than Optimizer) and uses `converged`, and any Optimizer implemented outside ASE that used the new version of `converged`.
As it reverts a recent API break that might please more people than it annoys. I think the release note needs to be emphatic that this changes the behaviour of `converged()`.
comments.label_reasoning: The comment discusses inheritance hierarchy concerns (Dynamics vs Optimizer), API compatibility breaks, and class design decisions around method availability and behavior.

review_threads.actionability_reasoning: Flags that the release note needs to be more emphatic about behavior changes, and raises concerns about breakage for code inheriting Dynamics — both imply needed changes.

comments.author: yuzie007
comments.body:
Thank you @askhl and @ajjackson for further explanation! I think I can also mostly understand the motivation and agree on the way to recover the old `converged` behavior.

While it does not very directly related to the present MR, I just got one question about the `Optimizable` design. Now it has
```python
    def gradient_norm(self, gradient):
        forces = gradient.reshape(-1, 3)  # XXX Cartesian
        return np.linalg.norm(forces, axis=1).max()
```
where the reshaping the gradient seems to me a domain knowledge to be rather in `OptimizableAtoms`.
Is it somehow planned to move this to `OptimizableAtoms`, or do I misunderstand something?
comments.label_reasoning: The comment questions whether domain-specific knowledge (Cartesian reshape logic) belongs in the base Optimizable class or should be moved to OptimizableAtoms, which is a class design/encapsulation concern.

comments.author: askhl
comments.body:
If we like it better, we can also refrain from changing this again.  But here we go:

Previously most implementations defined either `def converged(forces=None)` or `def converged(f=None)`.  IIRC the actual superclass had `def converged(self): pass` but that was ignored by all the subclasses.  The keywords have never been consistent but probably everyone who actually passed forces would pass them positionally anyway.

What we can do for maximal compatibility is `def converged(forces=None)` which reshapes automatically so it does not care about Nx3 versus flat layout, and also, it doesn't care about the sign because it calculates a norm.  That way it'll be the same if someone passes flat gradient or Nx3 forces, and of course it'll also work when nothing is passed.

We could make that change, then leave it at that, and focus on ASE4 API for further improvements.

comments.author: askhl
comments.body:
@miro.ilias Those are on Optimizable, i.e., not Optimizer.  They are meant to be like that.

The Optimizable is what the Optimizer is optimizing.  It is better for the Optimizable to know things like whether it converged, because the Optimizer doesn't know *what* it is optimizing (Atoms, NEB, some other function) whereas the Optimizable would know and hence implement a reasonable criterion (e.g. knowing differences between stresses and forces).  But even the Optimizable interface does not fully disentangle the knowledge, we try to do that in !3941 (still just a prototype, may not be easy to understand currently)

comments.author: askhl
comments.body: So the opt.converged() just calls the Optimizable in a way that makes it work as before.

comments.author: askhl
askhl
comments.body:
> I think the release note needs to be emphatic that this changes the behaviour of `converged()`

It will only break the most recent behaviour in the case where the gradient was explicitly passed as a keyword.  That could also be avoided by having an *additional* optional `gradient=` keyword.

comments.author: askhl
comments.body:
It *should* basically be an abstract method yes.  It must necessarily be overridden by an optimizable that has non-divisble-by-three DOFs.  The thing is, all current optimizables do this the same way so the price of making it abstract now is that we'll duplicate it in many places.

Thanks @yuzie007, I'll merge.

comments.author: ajjackson
comments.body: @yuzie007 The issue with that scheme is it requires changes on both sides: the `converged(gradient)` function needs modifying to provide a default argument (currently `gradient` is mandatory) and the user code needs modifying to stop passing the forces.

thread.actionability_reasoning: Explains why the current approach requires changes on both sides — clarifying context, not requesting a code change.
